title: TypeScript Functions Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on typing TypeScript functions: parameter and return types, optional, default and rest parameters, overloads, this parameters, function types and call signatures, and void vs undefined.

chapters.title: Typing Parameters and Returns
points: Parameters need explicit annotations, since they are implicitly any under noImplicitAny: function add(a: number, b: number): number
Return types are inferred from the body; annotate them on exported or public functions to lock the contract and catch accidental changes
Arrow functions take the same annotations: const f = (x: string): number => x.length
Destructured parameters are annotated on the whole object: function f({ id, name }: { id: number; name: string })
A function that never returns normally (throws or loops forever) has return type never

chapters.title: Optional, Default and Rest Parameters
points: Optional parameter: name?: T makes the type T | undefined, and it must come after the required parameters
Default parameter: function f(x = 10) infers x: number, makes it optional for callers, and applies only when the argument is undefined
Passing null does not trigger a default, and neither does 0 or an empty string; only undefined does
Rest parameter: function sum(...nums: number[]) must be last and must be an array or tuple type
Spread a tuple into a call by typing the rest as a tuple: function f(...args: [string, number])

chapters.title: Function Types and Call Signatures
points: Function type expression: type Fn = (a: number, b: number) => number; parameter names are only documentation and do not need to match
Call signature in an object type: type Fn = { description: string; (x: number): string } describes a callable that also has properties
Construct signature: type Ctor = new (x: string) => Foo describes something callable with new
Parameter bivariance is closed by strictFunctionTypes: with strict on, function-type parameters are checked contravariantly
A function with fewer parameters is assignable to a type with more, so callbacks may ignore extra arguments: [1,2].forEach(x => ...) is fine

chapters.title: Overloads and this Parameters
points: Overload: write several signatures with no body, then one implementation signature: function f(x: string): string; function f(x: number): number; function f(x: any) { return x }
The implementation signature is not visible to callers; only the overload signatures are callable
Order overloads from most specific to least specific, because the first matching signature wins
Prefer a union parameter or a generic over overloads when the return type does not depend on which argument type is passed
this parameter: a fake first parameter that is erased at compile time, e.g. function f(this: HTMLElement, e: Event); calling it with the wrong this is an error

chapters.title: void vs undefined
points: void means the return value should be ignored; undefined means the function really returns the value undefined
A function typed () => undefined must contain an explicit return undefined (or return nothing only if the return type is void), while () => void accepts any function
A callback typed () => void may return something else, and the result is discarded: const f: () => void = () => 42 is allowed
A function declaration written with an explicit : void return type cannot return a value; the escape applies only to function type assignment
Do not use void in a union with other return types like string | void; use undefined instead
Use void for callback return types such as forEach, so passing a function that returns a value, e.g. arr.push, still type checks

chapters.title: TypeScript Functions Cheat Sheet
points: Optional x?: T, default x = v, rest ...xs: T[]: required first, optional or default next, rest last
Overloads: signatures with no body, then one implementation signature that callers cannot see; most specific first
Callable type: (a: A) => R for a plain function, { (a: A): R; prop: P } for a callable with properties, new (a: A) => R for a constructor
this parameter: function f(this: T, ...) is compile time only and is not counted as an argument
void for ignored results, undefined for a real undefined value, never for a function that does not return
Common mistakes: implicit any on parameters, passing null expecting a default, wrong overload order, void in a union, a required parameter after an optional one
